statement: A solid has 14 flat faces: 6 squares and 8 triangles. Every edge of the solid is a side of exactly one square and exactly one triangle. How many edges does the solid have?

choices.misconception: I counted the $6 \times 4 = 24$ sides of the squares and halved them, as if two squares met at every edge.
I counted the faces of the solid instead of its edges.
I added the 24 square sides to half of the 24 triangle sides, halving only the triangles.
I added all $6 \times 4 + 8 \times 3 = 48$ sides but forgot that each edge is a side of two faces, so every edge was counted twice.

hints: Every edge is a side of how many faces?
Count all the sides of all the faces, then ask how many times each edge was counted. Overcounting on purpose and then correcting is often the quickest way.
The squares have 24 sides and the triangles have 24 sides, 48 in all. Each edge is one square side and one triangle side.

solutions.reliable: Count sides face by face: the 6 squares have $6 \times 4 = 24$ sides and the 8 triangles have $8 \times 3 = 24$ sides, 48 sides in all. Every edge is a side of exactly two faces (one square and one triangle), so each edge was counted twice. The solid has $48 \div 2 = 24$ edges. The transferable idea: overcount in an easy way, then divide by how many times each object was counted.
solutions.elegant: Every edge belongs to exactly one square, so the sides of the squares alone list each edge exactly once: $6 \times 4 = 24$. The triangles give the same count, $8 \times 3 = 24$, which is a free check. When one family of faces sees each edge exactly once, count that family alone.

whyOnTest: Counting edges through faces is a classic overcount: each edge is shared by two faces, so you must divide, or find a family that sees each edge once.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
